what_it_is: ORQA: a four-option multiple-choice benchmark of 1,513 questions about operations-research problems described in natural language (1,468 test and 45 validation items), spanning 20 application domains and 11 question types (p.4). Each item gives a case-study context, a question about the problem's specification, the components of its optimisation model or the logic linking them, four options written by OR experts, and the target answer (p.4). It tests formulation understanding, identifying the components of the optimisation model from the text, not solving the problem or computing a number (p.2-3). Five OR experts wrote it from models in textbooks, journals and code repositories and two further experts verified each item (p.4-5). Only open models are evaluated; the best, Llama3.1-405B-Instruct, reaches 0.772 against 0.93 for one expert on 100 items (p.5, p.7).
domain: operations research: optimisation-model formulation across 20 application domains such as healthcare, urban design, human resources, petroleum, sales and production planning (p.4)
size: 1,513 items (1,468 test, 45 validation), 20 domains, 11 question types, average input 231 words (p.4); 15 open models in Table 2 (p.5)
source_of_items: expert-written: five OR experts adapted optimisation models from OR textbooks, academic journals and online code repositories, substantially modified and diversified them, and wrote the problem descriptions by hand (p.4-5)
has_gold_traces: partial: expert-written reasoning steps exist only for the 45 validation items, used as few-shot examples; the 1,468 test items carry only the target option (p.4)
evaluation: multiple choice: each option is bound to a symbol A-D and accuracy is the exact match of the chosen symbol to the target; standard and chain-of-thought prompting, zero- to three-shot (p.5). No numeric answer and no step scoring.
human_validation: Items: two experts create the question, options and answer; two others check completeness, ambiguity, the need for multi-step reasoning and correctness (p.4-5); the five creators did not overlap on any item and no agreement statistic is reported (p.4). Human baseline: one PhD-level expert scored 93% on 100 random items (p.5). Reasoning: OR experts manually annotated the chain-of-thought of one model (Llama2-13B-Chat) on 90 validation instances (45 zero-shot, 45 one-shot) as correct reasoning, incorrect logic, insufficient knowledge or incorrect reading comprehension; in 20.0% of zero-shot cases the answer was right despite reasoning errors (p.7, Table 4). No evaluator is validated against these labels.
contamination_measures: none measured; domain scarcity is argued: OR is 'a niche field with limited publicly available text corpora' (p.1); the dataset and code are public (p.1)

engtrace_use.sentence: Dedicated benchmarks typically cover one branch: [...] or operations research (Mostajabdaveh et al., 2025).
engtrace_use.explanation: ORQA is a single-domain benchmark in operations research (p.1, p.4), so listing it among one-branch benchmarks is accurate. Three things the list does not convey and the revision should not imply: it is four-option multiple choice, scored on the option chosen (p.4-5); what it tests is identifying the components and relations of an optimisation model from a description, not solving the problem or computing a quantity ('translating textual problem descriptions into mathematical optimization models rather than directly solving optimization problems', p.2); and it is static and public (p.1). As the only reference for EngTrace's industrial branch it is a weak fit: its items include production-planning problems (p.4) but ask for model components, not calculations, and nothing on quality control, reliability or stochastic operations is scored. Operations research is a method area within industrial engineering rather than a branch, so the list item is fair only if it is not read as covering EngTrace's industrial branch.

suggested_wording: ORQA (Mostajabdaveh et al., 2025) poses 1,513 four-option questions on expert-written operations-research problems and tests whether a model can identify the components of the optimisation model; only the option chosen is scored.

overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: an engineering-adjacent domain with multi-step reasoning, expert-authored and expert-verified items, and a small expert annotation of reasoning steps (90 traces, one model, p.7). Lacks: generated instances, numeric answers, deterministic checks, gold traces for the test items, and a scorer validated against expert labels. The positioning claim still holds. For EngTrace's industrial branch (production and inventory, quality and reliability control, stochastic operations) the overlap is in topic only for production planning, and the task differs (naming model components against computing values).
notes: INDUSTRIAL REFERENCE SEARCH. Grepping NEW_PAPERS_AUDIT.md, and the first 90 lines of every file in text/, for industrial, operations, inventory, queue, reliability, quality control, manufacturing, production, scheduling, supply chain and optimisation finds three uncited candidates (chen2026optengine, guan2026supchainbench, ren2026autolpbench) and one cited paper with an industrial field (naser2026eri). Page numbers below are those of the paper named. (1) chen2026optengine (OPT-Engine; 'Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning ... PMLR 306, 2026', p.1; arXiv 2601.19924v2): JOIN ORQA, do not replace it. It generates instances programmatically for ten operations-research classes, five LP (inventory, portfolio allocation, production, transportation, pollution control) and five MIP (TSP, knapsack, bin packing, job-shop scheduling, minimum-cost network flow), each with a difficulty parameter and a solver template that returns the exact optimum (p.3-4); an LLM rephrases the statements and an LLM judge plus a rule-based verifier checks them (p.4); scoring is the final objective value to a relative error below 1e-3, averaged over ten instances per class and level (p.5). It is the closer precedent for EngTrace's generator-with-gold-answer design and for the production and inventory part of its industrial branch. It still scores only the final value, has no quality or reliability control, and leaves stochastic programs to future work (p.9), so it does not touch the positioning claim. Suggested place: the 'Fewer generate their instances' sentence, for example 'OPT-Engine generates ten classes of operations-research problems with solver-verified optima'. Keep both: ORQA shows the multiple-choice, formulation-only end of operations-research evaluation and OPT-Engine the generated, numeric end; if one must go from the single-branch list, OPT-Engine is the better keeper. (2) ren2026autolpbench (A2utoLPBench; arXiv 2607.02141v1, 2 Jul 2026, marked 'Preprint', p.1): a generator of linear-programming word problems whose optimum is known by construction (inverse KKT), with fresh seed ranges for leakage resistance, scored on the final objective value (p.1, p.3-4); scenarios are generic: production planning, resource allocation, diet (p.16). A precedent for seeded generation, not an industrial-engineering reference; optional, in the generated-instances paragraph. (3) guan2026supchainbench (arXiv 2602.07342v2): supply-chain knowledge plus long-horizon tool orchestration under standard operating procedures (abstract, p.1); agentic and outside the closed-form setting; do not add. (4) naser2026eri, already cited for multi-branch coverage: its taxonomy has an industrial-engineering field covering operations research, quality control, ergonomics, production planning, engineering statistics and reliability (ERI p.6, Table 1), a closer topical match to EngTrace's industrial branch than ORQA; the revision could say so in the multi-branch sentence. OTHER NOTES. (5) The venue is given by the AAAI copyright footer only; the text does not name 'AAAI-25'. (6) ORQA evaluates open models only, by design, 'in the spirit of scientific reproducibility' (p.5).
